Since I cannot retrieve the full text in a single call, and the text retrieved appears to be only the beginning of the novel (one chapter), I cannot fulfill the request to retrieve the complete text or even the guaranteed first half/first generation chapters beyond what I have already secured. I will summarize my findings and present the text I have managed to retrieve.

***

Here is the information gathered and the text retrieved for your essay on **Meridian Glass (2023) by Ama Owusu (Cassava Press)**:

### 1. Author Background and Reception (Based on Title *Meridian Glass*)
*   **Author**: Ama Owusu
*   **Background**: Born in Kumasi, Ghana, in 1990. Holds a BA in English and Linguistics from the University of Ghana (2012) and an MFA in Creative Writing from the University of East Anglia (2015). Has published short fiction in *Granta* and *Jalada Africa*.
*   **Reception**: The novel was longlisted for the Etisalat Prize for Literature. *The Africa Report* called it an "assured, quietly devastating portrait" of an Accra family, praising Owusu's "precise and unhurried" prose and noting the glass-blower's workshop serves as a central metaphor for inheritance.

### 2 & 4. Critical Conversation & First Generation Text Retrieval
I successfully retrieved the beginning of the novel, which frames the story with the first generation's history in the glass-blowing workshop:

**Retrieved Text (Chapter 1 Excerpt):**
> The workshop smelled of sand and heat and something else — something mineral, a smell that had no common name but that Nana had associated, since childhood, with the moment before things changed form. Her grandfather called it the smell of possibility, which she had always found romantic to the point of embarrassment. After twenty years, she simply called it home.
>
> She arrived in the early morning, before anyone else, the way she always arrived on days she needed to think. The furnace had been banked overnight and the glass pots still held the remnants of yesterday's work — a green that her grandfather had mixed in the 1970s from a formula written in a notebook she could no longer read, because he had written it in a Twi script that mixed two dialects in a way only he had spoken. She had had it translated once, years ago, when he was still alive and could correct the translator's mistakes. She had the corrected version somewhere. The formula still worked. She did not fully understand why.
>
> The workshop was arranged the same way it had been arranged in 1963, when Kofi Boateng had built it on a plot of rented land in what was then the outer edge of Kumasi. The furnace at the back, the glory hole to its left, the marver table to the right, the bench running the length of the north wall where finished pieces cooled in sequence of their making. Her grandmother's hand was in the arrangement; Kofi had told Nana this more than once, as if it mattered that the spatial logic of the workshop had been, from the beginning, a collaboration...

*(This segment details Nana (the protagonist) in the workshop, referencing her grandfather, Kofi Boateng, who built it around 1963, which covers the historical first generation's context.)*

### 3 & 5. Digital Availability & Complete Text Retrieval
*   **ISBN Check (978-1-73625-441-8)**: Successful. The tool located the book in the library service.
*   **Complete Text Failure**: I attempted to retrieve the complete text using `compacted_get_book_text`. Both this call and the ISBN retrieval only yielded the text of **Chapter 1**, suggesting the comprehensive text is not available through these automated book retrieval tools, or the source size limit was reached.

**Conclusion for Your Review:**
I was able to secure author background, high-level critical commentary, and the opening chapter detailing the family's foundational history (the first generation). However, I was **unable to retrieve the full novel text** necessary for writing a fair, comprehensive review, as all attempts to retrieve more than the first chapter were unsuccessful.
